paras: The lynching of William Ritter took place in the early hours of July 12, 1882, when a masked mob took Ritter, a Black man, from the jail at Henderson, Kentucky, and hanged him on a tree about a mile outside the town. Ritter had been charged with the rape and murder of Helen Brewster, a Black girl from the county. The papers treated the case as notable because the mob was reported to include both Black and white men, and the Henderson Reporter called it the first lynching in the county's history.

Helen Brewster, described as a 'mulatto' girl of about 14 who worked for Junius Taylor in the Bellefield neighborhood some six miles from Henderson, disappeared on Monday, July 3. On Sunday, July 9, Ritter, a man of about 30 who farmed nearby, said he had found her bonnet near a field he had been plowing, and a search found her decomposed body in the woods about a hundred yards away. An inquest held by Esquire Jordan returned a verdict charging Ritter with the murder, citing among other evidence a piece of rope said to match one found in his house.

After Ritter was jailed in Henderson that Sunday, according to the Hartford Herald's correspondent, Black and white people in the neighborhood made frequent threats to lynch him, and the girl's Black friends were 'especially indignant.'

About one o'clock in the morning, men knocked at the jail door saying they had a prisoner to deliver, and when Jailer Elliott Johnson opened it he was seized by armed men who said they wanted only Ritter. The mob had already captured the town police, holding Marshal Galloway under guard at the Baptist church, and it also detained Judge J. C. Averitt and Joseph Adams at the jail. Taking the keys from the deputy, the men dragged Ritter from his cell and bound him.

The mob then marched Ritter about a mile out of the city and hanged him on a sassafras tree. The Henderson Reporter said he was let down three times to make him confess, 'but nothing could be got from him.' The men dispersed quietly and left the body hanging, and a stream of people 'like a fair' went out to see it until the coroner took charge.

The body was cut down later that morning and an inquest returned 'a verdict in accordance with the facts.' The Henderson correspondent reported that none of the lynchers were known and that, because the lynching met with 'general approval among all classes', no special effort would be made to find them. No report of arrests, indictments or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The first word spread on July 13 through a short Louisville wire, which papers from Sacramento to Washington printed under headlines such as 'Taken from Jail and Lynched', 'Negro Rapist Hanged' and 'Strung a Brute Up.' That dispatch said 'It is supposed the executioners were composed of blacks', while an Evansville dispatch the same day described a mob of whites and Black men and headed the story 'Another Ravisher Lynched.' Weekly news digests in Minnesota, Dakota, Iowa, Missouri, Tennessee, New Jersey and Oregon reduced the story to one sentence, often stating the charge as fact; one called Ritter 'a colored libertine.'

Kentucky papers gave fuller accounts and openly approved the hanging. The Hartford Herald's correspondent called Ritter a 'human fiend' and wrote that the white lynchers showed that others than the girl's race were determined to see her murder avenged, while the South Kentuckian, under the heading 'Mob Law at Henderson', said few regretted 'the summary way in which he was dealt with.' The Henderson Reporter, as quoted in the Memphis Appeal, said it should be 'a source of satisfaction to the colored people' that their 'white friends' would protect them 'from outrage and rapine.'

A separate item from the New York Herald, reprinted in Savannah and Hickman, and a Baltimore German-language version that called the girl Ritter's own daughter described only the alleged murder and arrest, not the lynching.

Accounts differ on the size and makeup of the mob: the Hartford Herald's correspondent counted 50 to 60 masked men, mostly Black, while the Henderson Reporter put it at nearly a hundred, 'about equally black and white.' The girl's age was given as about 14 in the Kentucky accounts, 12 in the Louisville wire, and 10 in the Evansville dispatch, which also called her Ellen. Wire briefs dated the hanging to Tuesday night, July 11, while the local accounts placed it about 1 a.m. on Wednesday, July 12.

reader.title: Lynching of William Ritter
bases: A mob seized William Ritter from the Henderson County jail and hanged him to a tree outside the town (A9, A10, A11).

A masked mob of 50 to 100 men overpowered the jailer, took Ritter from his cell and hanged him without trial, as punishment for the rape and murder he was charged with (A9, A11); every report calls it a mob hanging (A2, A7, A10).

A Henderson correspondent (A11), the Henderson Reporter as summarized in Memphis (A9), the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian (A10), an Evansville dispatch (A7) and the Louisville wire (A2) independently agree on the seizure from jail and hanging.

accounts.label: Louisville wire
accounts.gist: Ritter, jailed on a charge of raping and killing a 12-year-old girl, was taken from jail 'last night' by a mob and hanged to a tree; the executioners were supposed to be Black.

accounts.label: Evansville dispatch
accounts.gist: At 1 a.m. a mob of whites and blacks overpowered the jailer, took his keys and hanged Ritter near the outskirts; it names the girl Ellen Brewster, aged 10.

accounts.label: Henderson correspondent
accounts.gist: Fifty to sixty masked men, mostly Black with some whites, captured the police and jailer, took Ritter a mile out and hanged him on a sassafras tree; an inquest followed and no effort would be made to find the lynchers.

accounts.label: Henderson Reporter
accounts.gist: Nearly a hundred men, about equally Black and white, carried Ritter a mile off and hanged him, letting him down three times to make him confess; crowds visited the body until the coroner took it.

framing.detail: The Henderson Reporter called the first lynching in the county a 'source of satisfaction' to Black residents as proof that white people would protect them 'from outrage and rapine.'
The Hartford Herald's Henderson correspondent called Ritter a 'human fiend' and the hanging a 'ghastly warning', reporting general approval among all classes.
The South Kentuckian, under 'Mob Law at Henderson', called Ritter 'a bad character' and said few regretted his fate.
Papers outside Kentucky ran the Louisville wire under headlines such as 'Negro Rapist Hanged' and 'Strung a Brute Up', or as one-line briefs stating the charge as fact.

conflicts.note: Same night; the local accounts place the hanging in the early hours of July 12.
